tasks.intent: Show how the world's electricity was generated by source in 2023 — coal, gas, hydro, nuclear, wind, solar, and the rest — so I can see which sources dominate the mix.

data.description: Global electricity generation by source (TWh and share of total) for a single year, drawn from the Ember and Energy Institute electricity datasets.
data.shape: 8 categories x 1 quantitative (share of total generation)

expected.chart_family: sorted horizontal bar chart (shares of one total)
expected.key_insight: Fossil sources (coal + gas) still supply roughly 60 percent of world electricity, while solar and wind, though fast-growing, remain a small slice; the ranking from coal down to solar is the point.

failure_modes: pie or donut chart forcing the reader to compare angles and arc areas, which Cleveland & McGill rank far below position-along-a-scale for judging the coal-vs-gas gap
unsorted bars left in alphabetical or source order so the dominance ranking the question asks for is not legible at a glance

a rainbow / categorical-hue palette that assigns saturated unrelated colors to what is an ordered magnitude, adding no information and violating Bertin's separation of hue (nominal) from value (ordinal)
slices or bars that do not sum to 100 percent because 'other renewables' is dropped, so the part-to-whole claim is quietly false
3-D pie extrusion that distorts the apparent size of the front-facing wedges, an explicit Tufte lie-factor violation

tasks.intent: Break down US federal government spending for the last fiscal year by major function — Social Security, health, Medicare, defense, interest, and the rest — so I can see where the money actually goes.

data.description: Federal outlays by budget function for a single fiscal year, in dollars and as a share of total outlays.
data.shape: 9 categories x 1 quantitative (share of total outlays)

expected.chart_family: sorted horizontal bar chart, optionally a single stacked bar if the total-sums-to-one framing is the message
expected.key_insight: The big four mandatory categories (Social Security, health, Medicare, income security) plus defense and net interest account for the overwhelming majority of outlays; discretionary line items are individually small.

failure_modes: pie chart with a dozen thin wedges where the small functions become indistinguishable arcs, defeating the ranking task position-encoding would make trivial
a treemap whose rectangle areas are read imprecisely and whose aspect ratios bias size perception, when a bar's length along a common axis would be judged accurately
bars sorted alphabetically by function name rather than by magnitude, hiding the concentration that is the entire finding
categories that do not exhaust the total (no 'all other functions' remainder), so the parts do not sum to the whole and the figure misrepresents the budget
data labels showing raw dollar amounts with no percent-of-total, forcing the reader to do the part-to-whole arithmetic the chart exists to perform

tasks.intent: Show what the world died of in 2019 — the share of all deaths attributable to each major cause group like cardiovascular disease, cancers, respiratory infections, and so on.

data.provider: Our World in Data / IHME Global Burden of Disease
data.description: Global deaths by cause for a single year, as a share of total deaths, aggregated to top-level cause groups.
data.shape: 12 categories x 1 quantitative (share of total deaths)

expected.chart_family: sorted horizontal bar chart of cause shares
expected.key_insight: Non-communicable diseases, led by cardiovascular disease, dominate global mortality; the long tail of individual causes is collectively meaningful but individually small.

failure_modes: donut chart that makes the reader compare the arc lengths of cardiovascular vs cancer deaths, a magnitude judgment position-length encoding does far more accurately

a diverging red-green palette applied to a purely sequential quantity, which encodes no direction and fails for red-green color-blind readers (Ware on pre-attentive color, and color-vision-deficiency guidance)
leaving causes in GBD's internal ordering instead of sorting descending by share, so the mortality ranking is not readable
using a truncated or nonzero baseline on the value axis so small causes visually vanish and large ones look larger than their true share, a Tufte lie-factor problem
so many thin slices that direct labels overlap and are replaced by a legend, forcing back-and-forth lookups Gestalt proximity would avoid with labeled bars

tasks.intent: Show the age structure of the US population in 2020 — what share of people fall into each age band, split by sex — so I can see the shape of the population.

data.provider: US Census Bureau (2020 Decennial / ACS age-sex tables)
data.description: US resident population by 5-year age band and sex, as counts and as share of the total population.
data.shape: 18 age bands x 2 sexes (part-to-whole across bands, mirrored by sex)

expected.chart_family: population pyramid (back-to-back horizontal bars by age band and sex)
expected.key_insight: The US is no longer a young pyramid but a barrel — near-uniform working-age bands with a bulge at older millennials and a widening top — and the male-female balance flips toward women at older ages.

failure_modes: collapsing the age distribution into a single pie of broad groups, which discards the ordered age axis that carries the demographic shape
plotting male and female as two separate side-by-side charts instead of a mirrored pyramid, so the sex comparison within each age band requires eye-travel Gestalt symmetry would eliminate
reversing or scrambling the age axis so the ordered variable is not monotonic top-to-bottom, breaking the one encoding a pyramid depends on
using raw counts with inconsistent band widths (e.g. a lumped 85+ bar) without normalizing to a per-year rate, so unequal-width bins misstate the true density, a classic Tufte area-distortion issue
assigning a saturated categorical color to each age band as if age were nominal, when age is an ordered quantity and only the sex split should carry hue

tasks.intent: Show the global desktop and mobile browser market by share for the latest month — Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox, and the rest — so I can see how concentrated the market is.

data.provider: StatCounter Global Stats (public, redistributed via Our World in Data-style CSV)
data.description: Worldwide web browser usage share for a single recent month, across all platforms.

expected.chart_family: sorted horizontal bar chart of market share
expected.key_insight: The market is highly concentrated — Chrome alone holds roughly two-thirds, Safari a distant second, and everything else is a small combined remainder — a concentration story a ranked bar makes immediate.

failure_modes: pie chart where Chrome's dominant wedge and the near-equal small competitors force the hardest-to-judge perceptual comparison (angle/area) precisely where a length comparison would be trivial
leaving 'other browsers' out so the shares sum to less than 100 percent and the concentration is understated
bars ordered by brand recognition or vendor rather than descending share, so the ranking the question asks for is not encoded by position
brand-colored bars (Chrome multicolor, Firefox orange) that spend the hue channel on decoration rather than encoding the ordered magnitude, adding chartjunk in Tufte's sense
a truncated value axis or a 3-D exploded slice that exaggerates the leader's lead beyond its true share, inflating the lie factor
